newsitem.title: JAPAN: Prosecutors interested in Koike comments--lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors interested in Koike comments--lawyer.

text.p: Prosecutors are showing interest in statements by corporate racketeer Ryuichi Koike that three other major brokerages conducted illegal discretionary stock deals for him, Koike's lawyer said on Tuesday.
The three were Nikko Securities Co Ltd, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd, said the lawyer, Kyuzaburo Hino.
But no other brokers except Japan's "Big Four" and no other smaller brokers' names were mentioned by Koike, he said.

Industry sources said whether the alleged discretionary deals by Nikko, Daiwa and Yamaichi would become the subject of criminal charges depended on whether prosecutors or Japan's securities watchdog would be able to probe any illegal loss compensation in the discretionary transactions.
Hino said he did not know how Koike's new accusations would develop, but said prosecutors had shown interest in Koike's remarks on the three brokerages.

Koike is a key figure at the centre of a high-profile racketeer payoff scandal involving Japan's biggest brokerage, Nomura Securities Co Ltd, and one of the nation's top commercial banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd.
"I heard from him (Koike) that he had told prosecutors about the discretionary deals," Hino told Reuters by telephone.

Discretionary deals by brokerages for their customers are banned by Japan's Securities Law. But such deals would not be subject to any criminal charges unless they can be used by brokers to illegally compensate their clients for stock trading losses, the lawyer said.
Spokesmen at the three major brokers each said on Tuesday that they would not confirm whether Koike had accounts with them.
A Yamaichi spokesman said, however, that the company's internal investigation had so far shown no illegal deals.

A Nikko spokesman said the company had set up a committee to investigate allegedly irregular deals and improve its operations. Nikko plans to announce the outcome of its investigation once it is completed, he said.
A Daiwa spokesman said the company could not comment on the reported remarks by Koike as it could not confirm what he actually said.
Some industry experts, however, were sceptical about whether prosecutors would probe the other three major brokers.
"It would be nice if they'd decide to be thorough (about investigating other brokerages) but they may just decide to pound Nomura and forget the rest," said one lawyer who declined to be identified.
The financial industry has been talking about possible irregular deals between the three brokers and Koike as Koike reportedly owned shares in all the Big Four securities houses.
According to the Finance Ministry's investigation, DKB lent 3.16 billion yen to a company linked to Koike to enable him to buy 300,000 shares each in the Big Four in 1989.

Sokaiya buys stakes in firms to gain admission to annual shareholders' meetings, and extort money from the firms by threatening to ask embarrassing and sensitive questions about their business activities at the meetings.
